3. Defendant's case is that the transactions were out and out sale as the condition to reconvey the suit land has not been incorporated in the deeds of sale themselves and the deeds of agreement being separate and different one, the transactions do not come within the ambit of section 95(a) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. So the reliefs claimed for declaration as stated above and also for redemption, giving colour of usufructuary mortgage to the transaction, is not legally available. 

 4. The only question of law involved is whether the transaction namely, transfer of the suit land on the basis of deeds of sale accompanied by separate unregistered deeds of agreement to reconvey the suit land, effected in the same sitting, constitute the transaction as usufructuary mortgage as contemplated in section 95(a) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act after amendment of section 95 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act by the President's Orders No. 88 of 1972, 136 of 1972 and 24 of 1973 or whether the transactions are an out and out sale. It has been dealt with in different cases by the High Court Division as well as by the Appellate Division. The appellate Court below in this case on its findings that since the deeds of agreement were unregistered and the recitals to reconvey were not incorporated within the body of the sale deeds, the transactions cannot be called usufructuary mortgage, had dismissed the suit both for declaration and for redemption. 

 5. Mr. Shahidul Islam, the learned Counsel for the plaintiff petitioner, submits that although in t the case of AIi Ekabbar Faraji vs. Bangladesh represented by the Secretary Ministry of Land Administration and others (26 DLR 304), it was decided by a Division Bench that in a transfer by a registered deed of sale if the document itself does not contain the condition of reconvey the transfer cannot" be said to be usufructuary mortgage and it does not come within the ambit of section 95 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, but the said decision has been over-ruled by the Appellate Division in the case of Bangladesh vs. Haji Abdul Gani and others 32 DLR (AD) 233. 

 12. From the discussions above it is very much clear that transaction in question is a complete usufructuary mortgage for 7 years. The deed of agreement although not registered is admissible in law and as such, was legally accepted by the trial Court. It is on record that the deed of agreement 'was made an exhibit without any objection from the other side and in view of the provision of the decisions as referred above in 34 DLR (AD) 237 the limitation for redemption is 60 years. So from the very simple facts of both the parties in this litigation the findings and decision of the appellate Court below is the result of misconception and misinterpretation of the relevant law in the subject as to section 95(a) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, after having been amended by the aforesaid President's Orders. The decision of the appellate Court below, therefore, is not sustainable in law and it is liable to be set aside. Accordingly, the Rule is made absolute. The judgment and decree of the appellate Court are set aside and those of the trial Court are restored. The suit is decreed. Send down the records to the courts below at once.
